candidates.stem: The NCERT discussion in Chapter 7 shows that if the Moon is roughly 60 times farther from the centre of the Earth than the Earth's radius, then using the inverse-square form of Newton's law of gravitation the ratio of the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface (g) to the acceleration of the Moon in its orbit (a_m) is approximately:
candidates.explanation: From the universal law of gravitation (Eq. (7.5) in the NCERT excerpt) the acceleration produced by a mass M at a distance r is a = GM/r^2. Thus the acceleration at Earth's surface g = GM/R^2 and the acceleration of the Moon a_m = GM/R_m^2, where R_m ≈ 60 R. Taking the ratio g/a_m = (GM/R^2) / (GM/R_m^2) = (R_m/R)^2 = 60^2 = 3600. This agrees with the NCERT result shown (Eq. (7.4) giving a factor ≈ 3600). Option A (60) is incorrect because it uses the linear distance ratio instead of the inverse-square dependence. Option C (1/3600) is the reciprocal and therefore wrong sign of the comparison (it would represent a_m/g, not g/a_m). Option D (60^3 = 216000) is incorrect because it cubes the distance ratio rather than squaring it; the inverse-square law requires squaring the distance ratio, not cubing it.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Ch.7 §7.3 Universal law; Eq.(7.4) g/a_m ≈ 3600 (PDF p.4)
evidence_quotes: inverse square of the distance from the centre of the earth
candidates.notes: Calculation 60^2=3600 matches NCERT. Concept label is G-constant but tested inverse-square moon ratio — still within Gravitation unit.

candidates.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
candidates.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping down an inclined plane (as described in the NCERT excerpt). Which one of the following best explains why the cylinder has angular momentum (i.e., a rotational component of motion) about its centre of mass at any instant during the roll?

options.A: Because in rolling different particles of the cylinder have different linear velocities at an instant, so the motion includes rotation about the centre in addition to translation.
options.B: Because the entire cylinder moves with the same velocity at each instant, it is in pure translation and therefore has no angular momentum about its centre.
options.C: Because the point of contact with the plane is instantaneously at rest, the only angular momentum is about the contact point and the angular momentum about the centre must be zero.
options.D: Because only the translation of the centre of mass contributes to the motion; rotation about the centre does not contribute to angular momentum.

candidates.explanation: Correct answer (A): The NCERT excerpt explicitly describes rolling down an incline as a combination of translation and rotation and notes that in rolling different points of the cylinder have different velocities at an instant (e.g. points P1–P4 have different arrows in Fig. 6.2). Those differing particle velocities indicate a rotational motion about the cylinder’s axis (i.e. about the centre), so the body has an angular (rotational) component in addition to translation. Why the others are wrong: (B) contradicts the excerpt: pure translational motion is defined by all particles having the same velocity, but the excerpt shows that rolling is not pure translation—particles do not have the same velocity—so the statement that there is no angular momentum is incorrect. (C) is incorrect because although the NCERT text notes the point of contact can be instantaneously at rest for rolling without slipping, that fact does not imply the angular momentum about the centre is zero; the body still has rotation even though the contact point’s linear velocity is zero. (D) is incorrect because it denies the rotational contribution: the excerpt distinguishes translation from rotation (rotation about an axis produces differing particle velocities), so rotation about the centre does contribute to the motion (and hence to the angular character) of the body. The correct reasoning follows directly from the NCERT discussion that rolling is a combination of translation and rotation and that particle velocities differ during rotation.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Ch.6 §6.1.1 Fig.6.2 rolling = translation + rotation (PDF p.2,4)
evidence_quotes: all its particles are not moving with the same velocity at any instant
The rolling motion of a cylinder down an inclined plane is a combination of rotation about a fixed axis and translation
candidates.notes: A uniquely defended; B/C/D contradict NCERT rolling discussion.

candidates.topic: Kinetic Theory of an Ideal Gas
candidates.stem: Two containers of equal volume are maintained at the same temperature and pressure; one contains oxygen gas and the other contains helium gas (both treated as ideal). According to the kinetic theory ideas and statements in the NCERT excerpt on behaviour of gases, which of the following is necessarily true?

options.A: Both containers contain the same number of molecules.
options.B: Both containers contain the same total mass of gas.
options.C: Both gases have the same mean free path for their molecules.
options.D: Both gases must have the same viscosity.

candidates.explanation:
Correct (A): Avogadro’s hypothesis as presented in the excerpt and the relation PV = N kB T imply that equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules. The NCERT text explicitly states that equal volumes of all gases at equal temperature and pressure have the same number of molecules (and gives the standard number for 22.4 L at STP).

Why B is wrong: The total mass depends on the molar (molecular) mass of the gas. The excerpt states that the mass of 22.4 litres of any gas equals its molecular weight in grams at STP, so equal volumes of different gases generally have different masses unless their molar masses are identical.

Why C is wrong: The mean free path is defined in the excerpt as the average distance a molecule travels without colliding and is of the order of thousands of angstroms for gases, but its actual value depends on molecular parameters (size, spacing and collision frequency). The NCERT passage links molecular parameters to measurable gas properties, so mean free path need not be the same for different gases under the same macroscopic conditions.

Why D is wrong: The excerpt states kinetic theory relates properties such as viscosity to molecular parameters. Viscosity therefore depends on molecular characteristics (size, mass, collision behaviour) and is not guaranteed to be identical for different gases even at the same temperature and pressure.

evidence_quotes: Equal volumes of all gases at equal temperature and pressure have the same number of molecules
if P, V and T are same, then N is also same for all gases
candidates.notes: B contradicted by molecular-weight statement; C/D not guaranteed by NCERT.

options.A: For a liquid in equilibrium the pressure is the same at all points in a horizontal plane.
options.B: In a flowing fluid the pressure always decreases at locations where the fluid speed is larger (Bernoulli relation).
options.C: Bernoulli’s principle states that the total energy per unit volume of a fluid is the same at all points of the fluid, whether it is at rest or flowing.
options.D: Pressure in a liquid decreases with depth; the difference between pressures at two depths is given by P2 − P1 = −ρgh.

Why the others are wrong: (B) The excerpt notes that unequal pressure would cause flow but does not state the Bernoulli relation that links pressure and speed in a flowing fluid; that specific claim is not presented on the given pages. (C) The provided pages do not present a statement that total energy per unit volume is the same at all points or mix the cases of rest and flow; this formulation is not given in the cited excerpt. (D) This contradicts equation (9.6) in the excerpt: for a fluid at rest the text derives P2 − P1 = ρgh (pressure increases with depth), so the form with a negative sign is incorrect according to the given material.

candidates.subject: PHYSICS
candidates.stem: Two small homogeneous solid spheres of different materials are placed separately in a fluid and subjected to the same uniform external pressure. Based on the NCERT discussion of hydraulic stress, volume strain and Hooke’s law, which of the following is correct about their fractional volume changes and bulk moduli?

options.A: The sphere made of the material with the larger bulk modulus will show the smaller fractional decrease in volume under the same pressure; bulk modulus = (applied pressure)/(volume strain).
options.B: The sphere with the larger bulk modulus will show a larger fractional decrease in volume under the same pressure, because a larger modulus means stronger restoring forces produce more compression.
options.C: For a given applied hydraulic pressure, the fractional volume change is the same for all materials and depends only on the pressure, not on the material's bulk modulus.
options.D: Bulk modulus equals the change in volume per unit pressure, so a larger bulk modulus implies a larger absolute volume change for the same applied pressure.

candidates.explanation: Correct answer (A): The NCERT text defines hydraulic stress (equal in magnitude to the applied pressure) and volume strain as ΔV/V. It also states Hooke’s law (for small deformations): stress ∝ strain, with the proportionality constant called a modulus of elasticity. Applying this to uniform compression gives bulk modulus K = (hydraulic stress)/(volume strain) = (pressure)/(ΔV/V). For the same applied pressure a larger K therefore implies a smaller ΔV/V (smaller fractional volume decrease). Why the others are wrong: (B) is incorrect because a larger modulus means the material resists deformation more (so it compresses less), not more. (C) is incorrect because the fractional volume change depends on both the applied pressure (stress) and the material’s bulk modulus (the stress–strain proportionality), not on pressure alone. (D) is incorrect because it inverts the relation: bulk modulus is pressure divided by fractional volume change, not fractional volume change per unit pressure (the latter would be the reciprocal of the bulk modulus).
candidates.ncert_section_page: Ch.8 hydraulic stress/volume strain (p.2–3); §8.5.3 Bulk Modulus B=−p/(ΔV/V) (PDF p.7)
evidence_quotes: hydraulic stress ... equal to the hydraulic pressure
Volume strain = ΔV/V
B = − p/(ΔV/V)
candidates.notes: Larger B ⇒ smaller |ΔV/V| at same p. Factory evidence_pages omitted p.7 but claim is in same canonical PDF.

options.A: Humification leads to accumulation of humus that is highly resistant to microbial action and, being colloidal, serves as a reservoir of nutrients; subsequent mineralisation by some microbes releases inorganic nutrients from humus.
options.B: Leaching is the microbial breakdown of detritus into simpler inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide and water.
options.C: Decomposition rate is faster when detritus is rich in lignin and chitin because these compounds are readily used by soil microbes.
options.D: Low temperature and anaerobic (oxygen‑free) conditions accelerate decomposition because microbes are more active under such conditions.

Option C is incorrect because the NCERT passage explicitly says decomposition rate is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin. candidates.topic: Search for Genetic Material and Replication
candidates.stem: Which combination of experimental observations from Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase (as described in NCERT Class XII, Chapter 5 §5.2) provides the strongest, NCERT-supported evidence that DNA is the genetic material?

options.A: Avery et al.: purified DNA from heat‑killed S bacteria alone transformed live R bacteria into S, and treatment with DNase abolished transformation while protease and RNase treatments did not; Hershey–Chase: bacteriophages grown with radioactive phosphorus had radioactive DNA (not protein), showing that DNA — not protein — is the viral material that enters and directs infection of bacteria.
options.B: Avery et al.: the protein fraction purified from heat‑killed S cells converted R to S; Hershey–Chase: bacteriophages grown with radioactive sulfur (labelling protein) transferred radioactivity into bacteria, proving protein is the genetic material.
options.C: Avery et al.: RNase treatment abolished the transforming ability of heat‑killed S extracts, indicating RNA is the hereditary substance; Hershey–Chase: both radioactive phosphorus and sulfur labels were detected equally in infected bacteria, so both DNA and protein carry genetic information.
options.D: Avery et al.: heat killed S cells lost all transforming ability unless DNA was present, implying a non‑nucleic contaminant was responsible; Hershey–Chase: labelled DNA and protein both entered bacteria but only protein determined progeny virions, so protein is the genetic material.

candidates.explanation: Why A is correct: The NCERT account states that Avery, MacLeod and McCarty purified biochemical fractions from heat‑killed S cells and found that DNA alone caused transformation of live R cells into S; protease and RNase treatments did not affect transformation while DNase inhibited it. This identifies DNA as the transforming (hereditary) substance. The NCERT also describes Hershey and Chase labelling bacteriophages with radioactive phosphorus (which labelled DNA) or radioactive sulfur (which labelled protein) to ask which viral component entered bacteria, and presents these experiments as the unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material. Together these observations — loss of transformation after DNase and the phosphorus labelling of the viral genetic material that enters bacteria — support DNA as the genetic material. Why the other options are wrong: B contradicts the NCERT text: Avery et al. found DNA, not protein, caused transformation, and Hershey–Chase did not show protein (sulfur label) to be the transmitted genetic material. C is incorrect because NCERT reports that RNase did not abolish transformation (Avery’s results implicate DNA), and it does not support the claim that both labels were equally found in bacteria. D is incorrect because it misstates Avery’s conclusion (the transforming principle was DNA, not a non‑nucleic contaminant) and contradicts the NCERT summary of Hershey–Chase, which supports DNA — not protein — as the material determining progeny virions.

candidates.stem: A student reads that amino acids have an ionizable nature and that their structures change in solutions of different pH. Which of the following best explains why the ionization state of an amino acid changes when pH is altered?

options.A: Because the amino (–NH2) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups of amino acids are ionizable and can change their charged state with pH, producing different forms (e.g., neutral, zwitterion, or charged).
options.B: Because peptide bonds linking amino acids are readily broken and re‑formed at different pH values, changing the individual amino acid structures.
options.C: Because the R (side) group of every amino acid remains permanently uncharged, so only backbone groups determine overall ionization irrespective of pH.
options.D: Because only the R (side) group determines whether an amino acid is acidic or basic; the –NH2 and –COOH groups do not affect ionization with pH.

candidates.explanation: Correct (A): The NCERT text states that a particular property of amino acids is the ionizable nature of –NH2 and –COOH groups and that “in solutions of different pH, the structure of amino acids changes.” This means these backbone functional groups can exist in different charged states depending on pH (giving neutral, zwitterionic or charged forms). Incorrect (B): The passage describes amino acids and their functional groups; it does not state that peptide bonds are readily broken/reformed with normal pH changes. Peptide bonds form the polymer backbone but the explanation in the text for pH effects focuses on ionizable groups, not bond cleavage. Incorrect (C): The text explicitly classifies amino acids as acidic, basic and neutral (examples: glutamic acid, lysine, valine), so side chains (R groups) can be charged in some amino acids; they are not permanently uncharged in every amino acid. Incorrect (D): The NCERT passage says the chemical and physical properties of amino acids are essentially of the amino, carboxyl and the R functional groups, so both backbone (–NH2, –COOH) and R groups influence ionization; it is not correct to say only the R group determines acidity/basicity while the backbone is inert.

candidates.subject: CHEMISTRY
candidates.concept: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
candidates.stem: One mole of KCl (molar mass 74.5 g mol–1) is dissolved in 1.00 kg of water. The observed elevation of boiling point of the solution is 0.88 K. Given that Kb for water is 0.52 K kg mol–1 (as in the NCERT discussion of boiling point elevation), what is the van't Hoff factor i for KCl in this solution?
candidates.explanation: From the NCERT text, for dilute solutions the elevation of boiling point is proportional to molality: ΔTb = Kb · m. If the solute dissociates into i particles per formula unit, the effective molal concentration of particles becomes i·m, so ΔTb(observed) = i · Kb · m. Here one mole of KCl in 1.00 kg of water gives m = 1.00 mol kg–1, Kb = 0.52 K kg mol–1 and ΔTb(observed) = 0.88 K. Thus i = ΔTb / (Kb · m) = 0.88 / (0.52 · 1.00) ≈ 1.6923 ≈ 1.69. This is answer A. Why the others are incorrect: B (2.00) would correspond to complete dissociation of KCl into two ions and would give an expected ΔTb = 2 × 0.52 K = 1.04 K (as the NCERT example shows), but the observed ΔTb is smaller (0.88 K), so i is less than 2. C (1.04) confuses the expected ΔTb for full dissociation (1.04 K) with the numerical value of i; 1.04 is a temperature change (K), not the dimensionless van't Hoff factor here. D (0.52) is the value of Kb (Kb for water) and not the van't Hoff factor; substituting that into the formula would not match the observed ΔTb. Thus only A is consistent with the NCERT relations and the given data.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Solutions — ΔTb=Kb·m; van’t Hoff i; Kb(water)=0.52 (Ch. Solutions)
evidence_quotes: van’t Hoff introduced a factor i
value of i for aqueous KCl solution is close to 2
candidates.notes: i=0.88/(0.52·1)≈1.69 arithmetically correct. Observed ΔTb=0.88 K is a problem datum (not a quoted NCERT measurement); formula/constants are NCERT-supported.

candidates.stem: Which one of the following statements correctly describes an acylation reaction of a primary aliphatic amine as given in the NCERT discussion on reactions of amines?

options.A: Acylation of a primary aliphatic amine with an acid chloride (or anhydride/ester) replaces a hydrogen of –NH2 by an acyl group to give an amide, and the reaction is carried out in the presence of a base stronger than the amine (for example, pyridine) to remove the HCl formed.
options.B: Acylation of a primary aliphatic amine occurs with alkyl halides to give amides, and no base is required.
options.C: When a primary aliphatic amine reacts with a carboxylic acid at room temperature it undergoes acylation to give the corresponding amide directly.
options.D: Acylation of a primary aliphatic amine with acid chlorides proceeds without formation of HCl, so addition of a stronger base like pyridine inhibits the reaction.

candidates.explanation: Option A is correct because the NCERT text states that aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution in which a hydrogen of –NH2 or >N–H is replaced by an acyl group to give amides, and that the reaction is carried out in the presence of a base stronger than the amine (e.g., pyridine) which removes the HCl formed and shifts the equilibrium to the right. Option B is incorrect because alkylation involves reaction with alkyl halides (not acid chlorides) and gives alkylated amines, not amides; the NCERT explicitly distinguishes alkylation (with alkyl halides) from acylation. Option C is incorrect because the NCERT notes that amines form salts with carboxylic acids at room temperature rather than directly undergoing acylation to give amides. Option D is incorrect because the NCERT explicitly states that HCl is produced during acylation and that a stronger base such as pyridine is used to remove the HCl; therefore a base does not inhibit but facilitates the reaction.

candidates.stem: According to the NCERT discussion in the Chemical Kinetics unit on temperature dependence of rate and the Arrhenius equation, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: For many chemical reactions, an increase of temperature by 10°C nearly doubles the rate constant.
options.B: NCERT states that increasing temperature generally decreases the rate constant because molecular collisions become less effective.
options.C: For a first-order reaction, increasing the temperature increases the half-life of the reaction.
options.D: The NCERT example for decomposition of N2O5 shows that its half-life becomes longer as temperature is raised from 0°C to 50°C.

Thus option A matches the NCERT discussion. C is incorrect because for a first-order reaction the half-life t1/2 = ln2/k (given in the NCERT table); if temperature increases, k increases, so t1/2 decreases rather than increases. D is incorrect because the NCERT example for N2O5 decomposition gives half-lives that become shorter at higher temperature (10 days at 0°C, 5 h at 25°C and 12 min at 50°C), so the half-life does not become longer on raising temperature.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements about classification of carbohydrates and their reducing behaviour is correct?

options.A: All disaccharides are non-reducing because the glycosidic linkage always involves the reducing (aldehydic or ketonic) groups of the monosaccharide units.
options.B: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because its glycosidic linkage connects C1 of glucose to C2 of fructose, thereby involving the reducing groups of both monosaccharides.
options.C: Maltose is a non-reducing disaccharide because its two α-D-glucose units linked by a C1–C4 bond leave no free aldehydic group.
options.D: Ketose monosaccharides are non-reducing, while aldose monosaccharides are reducing.

candidates.explanation: Correct option (B): Sucrose is non-reducing because the glycosidic bond is between C1 of α-D-glucose and C2 of β-D-fructose; this linkage involves the functional (aldehydic or ketonic) groups that would act as reducing groups, so those groups are not free and sucrose does not reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagents. Why the others are wrong: (A) is false — not all disaccharides are non-reducing; only those in which the reducing (aldehydic/ketonic) groups are involved in the glycosidic bond are non-reducing (sucrose is an example), whereas others can be reducing. (C) is false — maltose (two α-D-glucose units linked C1–C4) is a reducing sugar because a free aldehyde group can be produced at C1 of the second glucose in solution, so it does show reducing properties. (D) is false — all monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, are reducing sugars; monosaccharides are defined as polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones and are capable of reducing reagents.

candidates.subject: CHEMISTRY
candidates.stem: According to the Crystal Field Theory description given in the NCERT excerpt (Class XII, Ch.5 §5.5), which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Crystal Field Theory treats ligands as point charges (for anions) or point dipoles (for neutral molecules), and the asymmetrical negative field produced by such ligands lifts the degeneracy of the metal ion’s d orbitals causing their splitting.
options.B: Crystal Field Theory describes the metal–ligand bond as arising from covalent overlap of metal nd and ligand orbitals and therefore ignores electrostatic interactions between metal and ligand charges.
options.C: The five d orbitals of a metal ion lose their degeneracy only when the metal ion is surrounded by a perfectly spherically symmetric field of negative charges.
options.D: Valence Bond Theory distinguishes between weak and strong ligands by predicting different extents of d‑orbital splitting, while Crystal Field Theory does not address ligand strength.

candidates.explanation: Option A is correct because the NCERT text defines Crystal Field Theory as an electrostatic model: it "considers the metal–ligand bond to be ionic arising purely from electrostatic interactions" and explicitly states that "ligands are treated as point charges in case of anions or point dipoles in case of neutral molecules," and that this asymmetrical negative field from ligands "lifts the degeneracy of the d orbitals" causing splitting. Option B is wrong because it contradicts the NCERT description of CFT: CFT is explicitly presented as an electrostatic (ionic) model, not one based on covalent orbital overlap (covalent overlap is the picture used in Valence Bond or Molecular Orbital approaches). Option C is incorrect because the NCERT excerpt says degeneracy is maintained when the metal is in a spherically symmetrical negative field; it is the asymmetrical ligand field that lifts (not a spherical field). Option D is false because the NCERT passage notes as a limitation of Valence Bond Theory that it "does not distinguish between weak and strong ligands," implying VB cannot predict ligand strength effects on splitting; by contrast CFT addresses effects of the ligand field (i.e., why different ligand environments give different splitting).

lifts the degeneracy of the d orbitals

candidates.stem: According to NCERT Class XII Biology (Ch. 7 §7.4), which of the following characteristics most clearly distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign tumour?

options.A: Ability to invade and damage surrounding tissues and to send cells via the blood to form new tumours at distant sites (metastasis).
options.B: Tendency to remain confined to the original location and cause little damage to surrounding tissues.
options.C: Retention of contact inhibition so that growth stops when cells touch neighbouring cells.
options.D: Very slow growth with no competition for nutrients with normal cells.

candidates.explanation: Correct answer (A): The NCERT states that malignant tumours grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding normal tissues and that cells sloughed from such tumours reach distant sites through blood and start new tumours there — this property is called metastasis. That invasive behaviour and ability to form secondary tumours is the defining feature of malignancy. Why the others are incorrect: (B) describes benign tumours — NCERT explicitly says benign tumours normally remain confined to their original location and cause little damage, so this is not a distinguishing feature of malignant tumours. (C) is incorrect because NCERT notes that normal cells show contact inhibition, whereas cancerous cells appear to have lost this property; retention of contact inhibition is not characteristic of malignant cells. (D) is incorrect because NCERT explains malignant cells ‘‘grow very rapidly’’ and compete with normal cells for vital nutrients, so claiming very slow growth and no competition contradicts the text.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Human Health and Disease — malignant tumours / metastasis
evidence_quotes: malignant tumors ... invade and damage the surrounding normal tissues
metastasis is the most feared property of malignant tumors
candidates.notes: B describes benign; C/D contradict NCERT cancer cell behaviour.

candidates.stem: According to the NCERT excerpt on Reproductive Health (pages shown), which statement best describes how national Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) programmes address infertility?

options.A: They create awareness and provide facilities, infrastructure and medical assistance for reproduction-related problems, explicitly including infertility.
options.B: They focus only on contraception and family‑planning measures and do not offer services for infertility.
options.C: They discourage medical interventions for reproduction-related problems and promote only traditional methods to manage infertility.
options.D: They use amniocentesis as a routine method to treat infertility in couples.

candidates.explanation: Option A is correct because the NCERT excerpt states that RCH programmes aim at creating awareness and providing facilities and support for building a reproductively healthy society and that strong infrastructure and professional expertise are essential to provide medical assistance and care for reproduction-related problems such as pregnancy, delivery, STDs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems and infertility. Option B is incorrect because the excerpt explicitly lists infertility among the problems for which medical assistance is provided under these programmes, not something excluded. Option C is incorrect because the text emphasises provision of medical assistance, implementation of better techniques and new strategies, and promotion of awareness rather than discouraging medical interventions or promoting only traditional methods. Option D is incorrect because the excerpt describes amniocentesis as a diagnostic procedure used to analyse fetal cells and detect certain genetic disorders, not as a treatment for infertility; therefore it is not a routine method to treat infertility.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Reproductive Health — RCH programmes list infertility among assisted problems
evidence_quotes: medical assistance and care for ... infertility
unprotected sexual cohabitation is called infertility
candidates.notes: Amniocentesis is diagnostic, not infertility treatment (D wrong).

candidates.subject: ZOOLOGY
candidates.topic: Origin of Life and Evidences for Evolution
candidates.stem: The passage describes several ideas and experiments about the origin of life. Which of the following best summarizes a conclusion supported by the experiments and observations reported in the passage?

options.A: Oparin–Haldane’s idea of chemical evolution in a reducing early Earth atmosphere is supported by S.L. Miller’s laboratory simulation (electric discharge in a closed flask with CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour) which led to the formation of amino acids, and meteorite analyses that found similar organic compounds.
options.B: Louis Pasteur’s sterile‑flask experiments proved that life can arise spontaneously from non‑living organic molecules under early Earth conditions, so spontaneous generation explains the origin of the first life.
options.C: Miller’s experiment demonstrated formation of complete living cells in the flask, thereby experimentally proving how the first cellular life originated on Earth.
options.D: Analyses of meteorites showing organic compounds prove that life arrived on Earth from outer space (panspermia), making terrestrial chemical evolution unnecessary.

candidates.explanation:
Correct option (A): The passage states that Oparin and Haldane proposed the first life could have arisen from non‑living organic molecules by chemical evolution in a reducing atmosphere. It also describes Miller’s 1953 laboratory simulation — electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour — and reports that Miller observed formation of amino acids. The passage further notes that meteorite analyses revealed similar compounds, indicating similar processes elsewhere. Together these points support the statement in (A).

Why the others are wrong: (B) is incorrect because the passage describes Pasteur’s experiments as demonstrating that life comes only from pre‑existing life — Pasteur dismissed spontaneous generation — so his work does not support spontaneous generation. (C) is incorrect because the passage reports that Miller observed formation of amino acids (organic molecules), not the formation of complete living cells; the passage explicitly says we have no idea how the first self‑replicating metabolic capsule arose. (D) is incorrect because, although the passage notes meteorites contain similar organic compounds and that panspermia remains an idea some astronomers favour, the meteorite evidence is presented only as indicating similar chemical processes may occur in space, not as definitive proof that life was delivered to Earth by panspermia.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Evolution — Oparin–Haldane; Miller 1953 CH4/H2/NH3/H2O; amino acids
evidence_quotes: S.L. Miller
formation of amino acids
reducing atmosphere containing CH4, NH3
candidates.notes: B/C/D contradict Pasteur/Miller/panspermia statements in NCERT.

candidates.subject: ZOOLOGY
candidates.stem: According to the NCERT excerpt on human reproduction, which of the following statements correctly contrasts spermatogenesis and ovum formation (oogenesis) in humans?

options.A: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues even in old men; it occurs in the seminiferous tubules where meiotic divisions of primary spermatocytes produce four haploid spermatids (23 chromosomes) which are transformed into spermatozoa. In females, formation of ovum ceases around the age of fifty years.
options.B: Both spermatogenesis and ovum formation begin at puberty and continue continuously throughout life in males and females, and meiotic divisions in both sexes always produce four equal haploid gametes from each primary meiocyte.
options.C: Spermatogenesis stops at about fifty years of age in males while ovum formation continues throughout a woman’s life; neither process is regulated by hormones.
options.D: Spermatogenesis in seminiferous tubules is driven mainly by FSH acting on Leydig cells to make androgens that directly cause release of sperms; female ovum formation is independent of gonadotropins and stops suddenly at age fifty.

candidates.explanation: Option A is correct because the excerpt states that spermatogenesis starts at puberty, occurs in seminiferous tubules where primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis to give four equal haploid spermatids (each with 23 chromosomes) which are transformed into spermatozoa; it also notes sperm formation continues even in old men, whereas formation of ovum ceases in women around the age of fifty years. Option B is incorrect because the passage explicitly says ovum formation ceases around fifty years, so female gamete production does not continue throughout life; the universal claim that both sexes always produce four gametes per primary meiocyte is not supported for females in the given excerpt. Option C is incorrect because it reverses the timelines (spermatogenesis does not stop at fifty; it continues in old men) and the passage describes hormonal regulation (GnRH → LH and FSH, androgens stimulate spermatogenesis), so the claim that neither process is hormonally regulated contradicts the excerpt. Option D is incorrect because it misstates hormonal roles: the excerpt specifies LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate androgen synthesis and FSH acts on Sertoli cells to stimulate factors for spermiogenesis; it is not stated that female ovum formation is independent of gonadotropins, and the hormonal assignments and mechanism claimed here contradict the provided text.
candidates.ncert_section_page: Human Reproduction — sperm continues in old men; ovum ceases ~50; spermatogenesis details
evidence_quotes: sperm formation continues even in old men, but formation of ovum ceases in women around the age of fifty years
Spermatogenesis starts at the age of puberty
candidates.notes: A uniquely consistent with NCERT contrast; B/C/D reverse timelines or hormone roles.

candidates.stem: A blood sample shows the presence of antigen B on the red blood cells and the plasma contains anti-A antibodies. According to the NCERT description of the ABO system, which option correctly identifies the blood group and the donor groups compatible for transfusion to this person?

options.A: Blood group A; compatible donors A and O
options.B: Blood group B; compatible donors B and O
options.C: Blood group AB; compatible donors AB, A, B and O
options.D: Blood group O; compatible donor O only

candidates.explanation: Presence of antigen B on RBCs together with anti‑A antibodies in plasma corresponds to blood group B (Table 15.1: Group B has antigen B and anti‑A in plasma). The NCERT table also shows that donors compatible with a recipient of group B are B and O (because O has no A or B antigens, and B has only the B antigen). Option A is wrong because blood group A has antigen A and anti‑B (not antigen B or anti‑A). Option C is wrong because AB has both A and B antigens and no antibodies in plasma; an AB person is a universal recipient, not the described case. Option D is wrong because group O has no antigens (and would not show antigen B on RBCs); although O is a universal donor, the sample described is not group O.
